segments.say: Lesson 18. Trees: B F S / Level Order. Queue-based traversal level by level: level lists, right-side view, minimum depth.

Breadth-first search (B F S) on a tree visits nodes level by level: the root, then all its children, then all grandchildren, using a queue. Here is an analogy. Ripples in a pond: the first ring, then the second ring, then the third, spreading out evenly.

Why does this matter? Anything "per level" (level lists, right-side view, averages) and anything "nearest / minimum depth". A few key words. Level: All nodes at the same depth. Queue: F I F O line: deck with append / popleft. Level size: len(queue) at the start of a level.
Level-order with a queue. Start with the root in a queue (F I F O: first in, first out).
Level size equals 1. Pop 4, record it, push its children 2 and 7.
Level size equals 2: pop exactly 2 nodes (2, 7) and enqueue their children. Snapshot len(queue) to know where a level ends.
Last level done. The last node of each level gives the right side view. B F S also finds the minimum depth first.

When B F S beats D F S. Anything "per level": level averages, zigzag order, right side view. Shortest path / minimum depth in unweighted structures: B F S reaches the closest nodes first. Use collections.deck for O of 1 popleft().
Template. Here is the code. Pause the video to read it line by line.

Let's compare. Structure: stack / recursion, queue. Order: deep first, level by level. Memory: O of height, O of width, up to n/2 leaves. Shortest path (unweighted): not directly,. Natural for: heights, paths, validation, levels, nearest, min depth.

segments.sec: Problem 1: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
segments.say: Problem 1: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal. Return the node values level by level, as a list of lists from top to bottom. For example, with 3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7, the answer is 3, 9, 20, 15, 7.

segments.sec: Problem 1: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
segments.say: The obvious brute force: D F S while passing the depth, appending each value to the list for its depth. Works, but B F S is the natural fit. That costs O of n. The smart way: B F S. Snapshot len(queue) to process one level at a time. Step by step: Put the root in a queue. Then, While the queue isn't empty: size equals len(queue), and pop exactly that many nodes into one level list. Then, Push each popped node's children.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of n space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

segments.sec: Problem 2: Binary Tree Right Side View
segments.say: Problem 2: Binary Tree Right Side View. Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Return the values you can see from top to bottom (the last node of each level). For example, with 1, 2, 3, null, 5, null, 4, the answer is 1, 3, 4.

segments.sec: Problem 2: Binary Tree Right Side View
segments.say: The obvious brute force: Build the full level-order list of lists, then take the last element of each. That costs O of n time, O of n memory. The smart way: Level-order B F S. Record the final node processed in each level. Step by step: Run level-order B F S. Then, Record the value of the last node popped in each level.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of width space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

A likely interview question: D F S versus B F S on trees? A strong answer: D F S (recursion or stack) goes deep, uses O of h memory, and suits path and height problems. B F S (queue) goes level by level, uses O of width memory, and suits level-based and shortest-distance questions.
